utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Zecevic, I note that Mr. Milutinovic is not with us. I take it we can continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he waived his presence for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Our next witness is Mr. Sladjan Pantic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document the usher will show to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly introduce yourself for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: My name is Sladjan Pantic, father's name Dragoljub, born 24 March 1969, in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell us briefly about your work history, employment history.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: My employment history began on the 19th of November, 1990, when I started a course of training to become a policeman, upon which completion -- upon the completion of which I was assigned to work in the department for internal affairs of Srbica as policeman in the police section of Srbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, look at me, not the screen. The people from the Victims and Witnesses Section only confuse you by instructing you to watch the screen and then you stop talking normally. It's better to keep eye contact. Where were you employed after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: After May 1992, or more precisely, in July I was transferred to the police section of Rudnik, which came under the jurisdiction of the department of internal affairs of Srbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did the police section of Rudnik cover?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: The Rudnik police section covered 18 villages, and our job was to maintain public order, enforce the law, and do the other things normally done by a police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Name some of the villages.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Let's begin with Rudnik itself, Kostolac, Kladernica, Leocina Turicevac, Brocna, Vocnjak, Radisevo, do I need to name them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That will do. Can you till us what was the ethnic composition of your police section?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: We were around 20, three among us were Muslims, Bahrudin Bandic, Ramiz Adrovic, and Ruzdija Milatovic, and there was another colleague working with us of Roma ethnicity, Ismet Kukac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have a good relationship with the local Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I was on good and even friendly terms with the entire population, including the ethnic Albanian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Albanians move out of Rudnik in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... go into the private session for a very short period of time. We should be mentioning some names, and for their protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan, do you have anything to say on that? Thank you. Very well, we shall go into private session for that reason.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, did Albanians freely come to the police section of Rudnik?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, they did not come freely because they were afraid of each other. If they were on good terms with the police, they would be boycotted by their own compatriots, and sometimes not only boycotted, sometimes there were worse consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then how did you get reports that a crime was committed, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: In informal discussions. In the street, in tearooms, in informal conversations when talking to Albanians, that's how we got our information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any drastic examples, that somebody was hurt or came to harm because they socialised with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that in Vitak village a man was killed by the name of Muhamet, his nickname was Barber. He owned a tavern, and he was killed on his door-step. We learned about it a few days later when his wife and son came to that tavern and Rudnik to collect the property from the tavern, to collect the effects. And when we asked, Where is the barber? They said he was killed outside his own house by people wearing KLA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, what was the ethnic composition in 1998 of Rudnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998 and before, Rudnik was a village with mixed population. There were some Serbs, some Albanians, and a very small number, perhaps two or three houses, of Romas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the picture we should have is of the Albanians moving out and the Serbs and Roma alone occupying the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, except that in one part of Rudnik itself there was a family by the name of Jovanovic. There were two or three houses there on the edge of the village, and those Serbs also moved out at the same time as Albanians because they were afraid to remain there alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998 were there any terrorist attacks in your area?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1998 too there were some, and the main road Pec-Kosovska Mitrovica was under blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1998 in which villages were there Serbs in your area out of the 18 villages?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Banje, Suvo Grlo, Rudnik village, Radisevo village, Kostrc, and Leocina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did Serbs move out, out of some of these villages on the territory of your police section?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: In 1998 Serbs from Radisevo, Kostrc, and Leocina left their homes, and there were no more Serbs there left after some KLA terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a road that was blocked. What was the category given to that road?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: It was a thoroughfare, a main road, from Pec to Kosovska Mitrovica, a continuation of the so-called Ibar motorway that continued towards Pec. And on that road -- let me say first that in some -- in Rudnik itself there was some trees that they felled to make them fall on the road and block it completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks on civilians and the police?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were attacks. On the local road from Radisevo towards Rudnik a Serbian family by the name of Deverdzic was attacked. A brother and sister were wounded in the attack. Also in Kostrc, Blagaj Jovanovic was killed outside his house. And on the road towards Leocina at the entry point to Leocina a woman named Dostana Smigic was kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the police ever attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: The police were constantly attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you stop sending patrols to a certain locality at a certain time; and if so, which locality?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give us the time, please.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I remember because it remained etched in my memory, on the 15th of August, 1997, during a regular patrol mission on the ground, we reached Vocnjak village, the hamlet of Ozren, where an Albanian I knew, a friend of mine, asked me, Why did you come here? And I explained why. He told me, Don't come here, take another path, KLA members are waiting for you and from this day on you will be attacked every day whenever you get out into the field. And from that moment on we did not go into the field in that area of about ten villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give us briefly the names of some of those villages where you no longer went, beginning with the 15th of August, 1997.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Kostrc, Kladernica, Turicevac, Brocna, Vocnjak, Izbica, Leocina, Donje Obilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was anyone else attacked after that day in an attempt to reach these villages, a state official perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the autumn of 1997 two tax men were in Vocnjak village where they were attacked by the KLA. Only they know how they managed to get out of there alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there an attempt to perform an on-site investigation after that incident and what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, an on-site investigation team went out of OUP Srbica, but they were attacked from all sides and they were unable to do the on-site investigation. Ljubisa Ilic, scenes of crime officer in OUP Srbica, was injured on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Let us focus now on end March 1999. Do you remember the assignment you received at that time. What was that assignment? Who gave it to you? Describe it.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I remember that assignment, it was passed on to me by the section commander based on the orders of Branko Jaradic, chief of the OUP, and that was to participate in an action to crush the terrorists, to rout the terrorists. They said I would be seconded to a unit from Belgrade that also included the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Describe, where did you set out from, how, and what a did you encounter on that first day, what was that day?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was the 25th. We gathered outside the station. The starting point was some 50 metres away from the station where the road starts towards Kostrc and on to Turicevac, and when I arrived that Belgrade unit was already there, and there was a tank. We set out towards Kostrc village, we entered it, and 7 or 800 metres on, we came across trenches and communicating trenches and then we were attacked by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So less than a kilometre away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... communicating trench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Communicating trenches -- well, they're like trenches, canals, some 30 to 40 metres in length. They're used for defence purposes, that's the term we use. Maybe there is another one in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Certain clarifications are required on occasion because of everything that is being interpreted. It wasn't your fault. You said that -- the 25th of and you meant the 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Less than a kilometre away from your starting point you were attacked, is that correct, some 7 or 800 metres? I'm just checking that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What followed after you were attacked on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: We were attacked and we responded, the fighting went on for about one, two, or three hours, then it stopped and we continued, although we were sniped at. We entered Kostrc village, we came to Dervisa Mahala and that's where we bivouacked the first night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you join anyone else along that route that day or was it the next day?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Not on the first day but on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the first day where did you go and who joined you?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: We went towards Kladernica village on the second day. We reached the outskirts of the village and turned to the right towards Leocina. On that path up the hill we were joined by another squad of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what kind of uniform was worn by the people of your group.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: The unit I was seconded to, the police unit, wore green camouflage uniforms with visible signs on their backs saying "police." Members of the army wore green camouflage uniforms. I was the only one to wear the standard-issue blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 26th of March, 1999, that is the next day?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: As I said, we turned to the right, we reached the plateau between Kladernica and Leocina villages. We entered the hamlet of Arije, and we spent the night in the first house we came across.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any fighting that day, on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: That day the unit I was with saw very little action, but to the left and to the right you could hear a lot of shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 27th what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: In the morning on the 27th, we got up and we were getting ready to go. At that point we were attacked from the village of Izbica. We responded and turned to the left, returning to a hill nearby so as to improve our position in relation to the KLA. After that attack, we pressed ahead towards Vocnjak village. So we used the higher ground to reach Vocnjak itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The make-up of that group, did it change as opposed to the 26th?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: It remained the same until we reached Vocnjak itself. Just prior to entering it, the military squad and the tank turned back and we pressed further towards Vocnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone on your route to Vocnjak?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: On our path to Vocnjak at the first elevation we came across we saw a column of civilians on the road moving towards the south. They were using the road and we followed them up to the outskirts of Brocna [Realtime transcript read in error "Brocna"] village. We moved along slowly, and as of the point when we entered Vocnjak village there were no attacks anymore. I don't know whether that was because of the civilians that were on the road or not, but in any case we reached Brocna village and we spent the night in Mahala Salja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the morning of the 28th, what happened and what followed that day?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: In the morning of the 28th we got up, to put it that way, since we were always ready to move. We waited for further orders, and during the morning - I can't recall exactly when - buses arrived, and we were taken to Metrohijska Klina. I was dropped off there and my role as a guide for those units was completed at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You and the group you moved with, did you have any contact with any civilians prior to the civilians you met on the road to Vocnjak?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, there was no contact with any civilians before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what PJP unit was with you?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I was with the unit that I have been told came from Belgrade. I don't know what unit it was specifically. I only know they were from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by the Prosecutor, who in this instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have some questions, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Cepic has some questions for you first of all. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pantic, good morning. My name is Djuro Cepic. I appear on behalf of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To go back to end March, you said that you were with the PJP unit and that they came from the -- from Belgrade. It was a squad. On the 27th when you were moving towards Vocnjak and along the entire route, did you and the Army of Yugoslavia squad you moved with entered the village of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, we did not enter Izbica village. We used a higher ground between Kladernica and Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the distance you covered starting from the village of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Well, the route we were following is some 800 metres away from Izbica itself. It's a forested hilly terrain. You cannot see much in front of you or on the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you see Izbica from the forest?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This military squad and the tank, they were moving behind you, they were following you?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: From time to time, the tank would have to choose its path, and the squad itself was sometimes closer to us, sometimes further away, but we all moved along together. I would say they spent most of their time following us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 27th of March there was an attack from several directions on the members of the unit you were with. Would you agree with me that those attacks were directed at the police unit and that the unit merely responded to the attacks?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: There was an attack, we responded, we responded. The tank was not engaged. There was shooting, and I didn't see where the people were exactly. I don't know whether the military infantry squad was firing back; however, I know that the tank did not fire that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One point of clarification, Mr. Pantic. You said that you -- when you encountered civilians they were using the road and you followed them up to the outskirts of Brocna village and then you are recorded as saying: "... and as of the point when we entered Vocnjak village there were no attacks anymore." Is that an accurate record of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we arrived there, we saw them on the road. We weren't following them per se. We saw them moving along that road, and that was the axis of our movement. We slowed down, waiting for them to pull out. During that period we were not being attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you at Vocnjak before you got to Brocna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We went through Vocnjak and reached Brocna village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And at what point was it that the attacks on you stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly. As far as I recall at the point of entry to Vocnjak, that's where the attacks ceased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Ms. Gopalan. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by asking you a few questions about the police station you worked at in Rudnik. You mentioned that there were 20 other policemen who you worked with in the station. Could you tell us why you were chosen to act as a guide for the VJ and MUP operations in late March?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I was chosen because I was the head of a sector, of the security sector, and I knew the terrain since I worked in that position for over five years. In Rudnik I worked as of June 1990 -- excuse me, July 1992 until the 19th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Were you the only guide for these VJ and MUP units in late March 1999 during the operation, or were there other guides?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was only me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What did you do as a guide?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: My assignment as a guide was to show them the way they have to take. They would tell me, We're supposed to go through Kostrc and to reach Kladernica, and then would say, Well, this is the route we are going to take. Then they told me, We have to go to Vis, up the hill to the right towards Leocina, and then I chose the path. I knew the local paths and that's why I was seconded to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said: "They would tell me ..." who gave you the instructions as to the route that the unit would follow?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. Specifically there was an officer there, although I cannot recall his last name. I was with him. He would be given instructions, I don't know from who, and he would simply tell me, This is the way we should -- we are supposed to go, and I would take them there, I would show them the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Was this a police or an army officer?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: He was from the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you describe to me the uniform this officer wore?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: He wore a green camouflage uniform with a flak jacket. On its back, there were visible letters saying "police." The uniform was camouflage green.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that some of the officers wore green camouflage uniforms. Did any of them have the wording "milicija" on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the term "milicija" stopped being used quite some time before that, maybe even up to two years before that. I know for sure that at that time we were the police, and that's what it read on our uniforms, we were policemen, we were not "milicija."

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I take it then that there were no -- you did not see anyone with such uniforms marked "milicija"?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So how big was this unit whom you were guiding, how many men were in it?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you an exact figure, but as far as I could see, it was a company, some 90 or 100 men. I am not versed in that, and I don't know what the regular company should comprise, but more or less it was the size of a company.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So the unit you were guiding comprised of approximately 90 to a hundred men who were either the police or the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. However, on the first day there was the tank and crew; and on the second day, a squad joined us of some seven, eight, or ten men from the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Were these men in any way differently dressed than the other army officers who had joined you at the beginning of the operation?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No. They were all dressed the same; however, the people in the crew were in the tank itself, so I couldn't see their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So when you were travelling with these units, how did you communicate with them? How were your instructions passed on to you? Were they handed to you verbally?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, there was the officer there, and I think he was probably a platoon commander. I was with him and he would tell me what we were supposed to do; and he would issue oral orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. So that was the only way, there were no radios involved; you just received your instructions in person?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So in terms of weapons carried by the men, did they have machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: We had usual infantry weapons, automatic rifles and pistols that each member had signed for, standard issue, that's all I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So you didn't see any machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did you see any hand-grenades being carried by the men?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I didn't, I don't remember. Perhaps they were carrying some, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: It's just that you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Maybe I don't remember but in terms of something that I could actually see them carrying hand-grenades on them, no, I didn't see that. I think I would have remembered. I don't know what they had in their pockets or in their flak jackets, but I certainly didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Was that because you were walking ahead from the unit or did you travel with them?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I was with them and every now and then I fell behind a little perhaps, but I certainly didn't walk ahead of them. That wasn't my mission. There was a lot of firing in the area, and I would not have relished the opportunity to be out at the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So was this the only occasion you acted as a guide for these units or any units for that matter?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Just that once.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: But even though it was only this one occasion, you're unable to recall the weapons used by those you were escorting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that I have to object, that this is misrepresentation. My witness explained exactly what kind of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What he said was what he saw, and you do have a statement by the witness so far of his recollection of what he saw. Now, are you challenging that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the witness has said that those with him had standard-issue automatic rifles and pistols. Now, what is it you're actually putting to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please, that would be better, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you do not remember that these men were carrying hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I never said they were not carrying hand-grenades. I said I didn't see them carrying hand-grenades, which doesn't necessarily mean that they weren't. I simply didn't see them. They didn't wear it on them. Perhaps they had it somewhere else. I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, you mentioned that -- I'm sorry, before I move on to that, do you happen to know which VJ unit you were escorting during this operation?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which VJ unit this was or who it belonged to. I didn't ask about that, I didn't talk to them, and I didn't know where the military had come from or which unit it was specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So you mentioned that on the 28th of March, 1999, you saw some civilians in the road in Vocnjak or close to Vocnjak. Could you tell us how many civilians you saw?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Not the 28th, the 27th, the afternoon on the 27th. I don't think I can be specific about the figure. They were heading down that road, and I really couldn't say. I can't be very specific. I could give you figures such as 100, a thousand perhaps, there could have been more, there could have been less, I simply can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And was that the only occasion on which you encountered civilians during your three-day tour?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only occasion over those three days that we encountered civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, we've had evidence in this trial that thousands of civilians were seen in the Izbica valley area around the 26th of March, a large number of civilian refugees --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And this for the purposes of the record is in the witness statement of Liri Loshi.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you still maintain that apart from this one occasion you did not see any other civilians moving in a large number during the time-period you were in the Izbica valley?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I didn't say that we were in the Izbica valley, nor were we, in fact. We were at an elevation between Kladernica and Izbica, and there was a forest between us and the valley itself. Therefore, we could not see if there were any civilians in the valley or not. The first time we set eyes on any civilians was the 27th, the afternoon of the 27th, as far as I can remember; they were walking down that road, and that's the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So from where you were on the 27th, you only saw between a hundred to a thousand civilians; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, I think you misunderstood me. What I'm saying is I can't say whether there was 100, a thousand, 5.000, perhaps. I simply couldn't tell. There could have been 2.000, 3.000, not that I could tell. They were walking down that road, but from where I was you could only see a limited section of the road, maybe only 500, 600 metres of the road, but you can't actually see any further than that, because there are bends in that road, there are forests over there, that sort of thing. I simply couldn't see. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So how many civilians did you actually see on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, I am telling you that I can't be specific, aren't I? I couldn't tell, so -- I don't know. In my opinion, I'm no expert. I can't tell you how many there were. There were some, they were walking down that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the part of the road that you could see, were there more civilians than there were police and army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So at least we know it was more than a hundred you could see. Now, can you help us a bit more specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps between -- more than a thousand, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's simply in the area that you can see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. There's an open view from this hill, you can see the valley and the section is about 500 or 600 metres long, as far as I remember; and that was the portion that I could see and I saw them walk down that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, we've had documentary evidence in this trial that approximately around the 28th of March, 1999, several thousand civilian refugees were expected in the Vocnjak village sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: For the trial record this is Exhibit P2046, it is a combat report dated the 28th of March, 1999, signed by the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade, Colonel Dikovic. I do not propose to show this exhibit to the witness, but I will simply say that the colonel has stated that: "In the forthcoming operations in the Vocnjak village sector, we expect to encounter shelters with several thousand civilian refugees."

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know why these civilian refugees were expected in the Vocnjak sector?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You would agree with me, though, that the village of Izbica is approximately 2 kilometres or less to the north of Vocnjak, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about north. The distance is about 2 kilometres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you were just outside the village of Izbica on the 28th of March with the units you were guiding?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the 28th. On the 28th we are still in the village of Blocnje. They came there to get us in the morning, they came with buses and they took us to Metrohijska Klina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sorry, is the village of -- could you please repeat the village you were at on the 28th, the name of the village, please.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Broc na.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Were you in Vocnjak at all?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: We passed through it on the way and then we reached Brocna. I said that already, we took the road through Vocnjak and we reached Brocna.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: After the 28th, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: After the 28th, after I had stayed behind in Klina, I went home to Siga village, Pec municipality, because that was the day my shift ended. In our department, we are facing a difficult situation and it was difficult to travel. So we only had five-day shifts. I would spend five days at the station and five days at home. I would, for example, spend five days at home, after which I would go back to the Junik [as interpreted] police station, and I would go about our regular, daily tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to another area --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just for the transcript, it might cause confusion, page 23, line 6, it's not Junik, it's Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other one that may cause confusion for all I know is Brocna. Is that meant to be, as far as you're aware, Mr. Lukic, the same village as Brocna?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are two different villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You go through Brocna to reach Brocna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is that the evidence is earlier recorded as, "going through Vocnjak to read Brocna."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every time should be Brocna, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you look at page 22, line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't want to jump every time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it that that name is not the name of a village in this area, B-l-o-c-n-j-a?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every time it's Brocna, it shouldn't be Brocna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now I would like to go back to mid-1998. Are you aware of any anti-terrorist operations conducted in the area of the 18 villages you mentioned earlier, your area, between mid-July 1998 and October 1998?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: At the time we were at the station. I'm just relying on my recollection. The main road was blocked and it continued to be blocked for up to two months. I know that there was a clearing operation, operation that was launched to clear that road. As for any other actions, I don't know if any other actions took place or not. My position was not such -- was not such that I would have known of any actions that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And was this action conducted by the MUP only or by the VJ and the MUP jointly?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that one action. The road is over 20 kilometres long, and we ourselves were at Rudnik. The road was being cleared from Rudnik to Mitrovica. I didn't realize what units were involved. I was, in a manner of speaking, just an ordinary police officer. I was not privy to that sort of detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, how could you distinguish a police officer -- a policeman, rather, from a soldier during the action between the 26th and 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Because of what their uniforms said. The police wore combat jackets, that's what we used to call them, and it said "police." And on the front side of their jackets they had a small pocket with a writing in white letters that said "police."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there more police than army in the action?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, more police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly what proportion were police?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, there was a police company involved, that was as far as I was able to see. As far as the military, I'm not sure about how big that tank crew was. There might have been a squad there, maybe seven, eight, up to ten soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have so far formed the impression that there were more soldiers than simply the tank crew; is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, no. That's not wrong. As I said before, on the next day there was a squad that joined us, a squad of the military, between seven and ten men in addition to the tank crew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I also had the impression that when you first met up with the team that there were soldiers there in addition to the tank crew; is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is wrong, I'm afraid. The only soldiers surrounding the tank were the crew, and they later got into the tank. Actually, they had begun to climb the tank already, but the commander of that crew was standing at the top of the turret. But there were no other soldiers in addition to those around the tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you -- sorry, when you joined the team, was the tank already there?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The tank was exactly at this position from which we then started out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who commanded this team in the action?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find that difficult to accept. Who commanded it?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: All right. I know and I said that, that I was attached, and there was a man from a brigade, I think he was the platoon commander, I was with that man. I don't know who he was receiving instructions from. It was above my head. I didn't know who was in command or who was issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The platoon commander you refer to, was he a policeman or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was this a police PJP unit or company?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a member of the PJP from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one was it, do you know the number of it?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see that. I don't think they actually had their number displayed on their uniforms. None that I saw at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you earlier indicated that it -- the strength of the police was about a company, but you talk about a platoon commander being in charge. Could you clarify that for me?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: The level was that of a platoon. It was from that level that I was seconded or attached to this new level to be in charge, and there was some platoon commander which in the roughest of terms -- well, what sort of manpower could he be in charge of, about 30 men. But in that company we had three such platoon commanders. There was only one that I was in touch with because I was there to work with him, to help him out. So it was he who told me where we should be headed, and he was issuing orders to me as to where we were supposed to go to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he issuing orders to the other two platoons as well?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who was in command of this action?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Overall, as I said, I don't know. I know they were from Belgrade. Those three men had their own superior officer whose name I do not know. I don't know. I couldn't see them all the time. They had some links, and they used radio links to communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe I read too much into your earlier answer, but I thought you told us that communication was by word of mouth.

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: By word of mouth, the link between me and him because that was the question that was raised as far as I remember, how I communicated with that, or rather, how he was issuing orders to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were sent from your own office to act as the guide, who were you instructed to make contact with when you got there?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: This was just outside the station, the police station, at Rudnik. This man that I was with, he came to the station and we headed out together pursuant to orders by my commander. We headed out some 50 metres, which is right outside the police station, and that's where we began moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who was this man that you met outside the police station?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: This commander, platoon commander, that I was with later throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he told you where you -- the names of the places you were to go to, but he didn't lead the other two platoons in the right direction, somehow or other that just happened; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I was with him as a guide. I was attached to this unit from Belgrade, the company, in that capacity. So we started out. They told me what my job was. They said let's go to Kostrc, and I would tell them let's take this path to get there. Who were they receiving orders from in terms of where we should go, now that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But as the result of you leading him in a particular direction, did the others follow in the same direction?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is how we went. We moved forward practically together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did he communicate with the army?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the tank travel behind you or in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: Depending on the situation and the road, the terrain, the first day as we were going on a kind of road they went parallel with us; the second and the third day he lagged a bit behind, more to the left or to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which brigade were the soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan, does anything arise from that for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only one question because of your questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Mr. Pantic. You were asked by Judge Bonomy whether there were more army troops or policemen. When you answered did you mean only your group or the entire action?

utterances.speaker: SLADJAN PANTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about the action as a whole. It's in the group that I was in that there were more policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for coming here to today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Pantic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, our next witness is Mr. Petar Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm told you might find it more comfortable to stand rather than sit. Which would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would sit for the time being, and if I need to stand up I'll ask your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's exactly what to do, so please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: My respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have some documentation here for you. We did not manage to put it in order yesterday, but we'll still try to go through it. It's easier than calling up documents on the screen sometimes. Can we begin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Damjanac, Savo is my father's name, mother's name Javanka Petricic born in Novo Cikatovo village, Glogovac municipality. I lived with my parents in 1966, or rather, 1969, when they were forced to leave our native village. I continued my schooling in the nearest town and did my university studies in Pristina. I found employment in the Republic of Serbia in the secretariat of internal affairs of Pristina. I started working as an inspector in criminal investigations in SUP Pristina. I was one of the senior staff in the crime police, and in 1991 in the notorious incidents when Albanians staged a walk-out from the police force, I was sent to SUP [as interpreted] in Glogovac, the department of internal affairs of Lipljan, as a head of the operative personnel. I worked there on that position in 1990 and 1991, when they pulled me back into my original work position, where I worked until end 1997 as chief of the crime police. When I was sent to SUP [as interpreted] in Glogovac, my hometown where I worked to the best of my ability until 1st May 1999 until the 16th of June I worked in the crime police. After the 16th of June, 1999, since our SUP was relocated to Niska Banja, 7 or 8 kilometres outside Nis, for family reasons because my family was living in Kragujevac at the time, from end June until the beginning of year 2000, I worked in Kragujevac; and after that I transferred to SUP Belgrade, section number 1, where I worked until retirement in August last year. That was my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Damjanac. I believe it is time for the break now. We will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, the system here is that we do have a break around this time each day. We will take that break for 20 minutes; while we have it, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that your Albanian colleagues walked out. Just before that it was recorded that you mentioned on page 31, line 21, SUP Glogovac. Was there a SUP in Glogovac or an OUP?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: It was an OUP, but it was territorially organized in Pristina as SUPs in municipalities. So when I find -- found work, I found work in the secretariat of Pristina which was under the jurisdiction of the municipality of Pristina, the city of Pristina, and it was linked horizontally and vertically with the MUP of Serbia through the provincial SUP but it was at the level of the municipality. Later it changed and it was called the security centre, former OUPs were called security centres. It was just a name change, but organizationally it was OUP Glogovac, linked to the SUP of Pristina or the security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So your Albanian colleagues walked out in 1990 and 1991, abandoning their jobs in MUP. What was the reason, why did they no longer work after that period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with the subject because I studied the statistics at that time. From 1964 until the end of 1989 and 1990, on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in terms of ethnic representation in the SUP, or rather, the MUP of the Republic of Serbia was 90 per cent of Albanians or Siptars, as they were called until it changed in 1969, and only 10 per cent conditionally speaking were non-Albanians, Serbs, Montenegrins, Turks, Muslims, the Gorani, Croats, et cetera. In 1989 Rugova's party was established called DSK when the multi-party system was introduced in Serbia. Already in 1989 a new platform took shape, geared at creating Greater Albania but through the institutions of the system. We have to bear in mind that this was soon followed by the amnesty of political prisoners led by Adem Demaqi and hundreds of others Albanian extremists who used the multi-party system to legalise their underground political organizations. In 1990 Rugova's party, the DSK, Rugova, and his associates an illegal Assembly in Kacanik, an illegal parliament called the Kacanik parliament, that happened sometime in September 1990. And that is when the constitution of the so-called Republic of Kosova was adopted. They formed all the institutions envisaged by the constitution, beginning with the government and all the ministries, the ministry of the army, the police, education, and everything else. And a demand was made at that time that all members of the ethnic Albanian minority working in state institutions, in health care, the education system, socially owned enterprises, and so on should abandon all the Serbian state agencies in order to form a parallel system with parallel agencies. Let me just mention that our colleagues, Siptars, I'll call them Siptars because officially we always called them like that and they called themselves Siptars, they demanded, although there was little media coverage of that, that parallel police stations be set up. In other words, that within one and the same system parallel structures would be formed. We, the Serbs, would be on one side and they, Albanians, would have everything of their own, their own barracks, their own everything. It is also worth mentioning the discipline that prevailed among this ethnic Albanian minority. In 1990 and 1991 as far as internal affairs are concerned, they all obeyed the order of their illegal leadership, their illegal parliament, of the already-proclaimed Republic of Kosovo, and walked out of their jobs in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, the autonomous province of Kosovo. I say Kosovo because Metohija was erased after the destructive demonstrations in 1968, and it was always called Kosovo from the liberation onwards -- it was always called Kosovo and Metohija from the liberation. There was a situation when the UN issued a document concerning health care where they said that although the majority of Albanian medical employees left their jobs and in 1998 the percentage they represented was 50.83 per cent. Most of the doctors and nurses were Albanians and 90 per cent of the patients were ethnic Albanians. In the education system, which was another burning issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure if I see the importance or relevance of this part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to deal with the -- this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's been interrupted now, so your objective has been achieved. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, I know you spent a lot of time studying this problem and you issued articles and so on and so forth, but we are limited in terms of time here. Therefore, please focus on my questions and try to provide brief answers to them. In relation to this topic, I wanted to ask you if you know of any specific examples of the names of people who left the MUP at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: Since, as I said, I was employed with the SUP in Pristina during that time and given that we had a very fair work-mate relationship, since we also associated out of office with our Siptar colleagues, we attended parties and funerals together, our mutual relationship was very good. Once that moment of separation arrived, it was very difficult for all of us and I believe for many of the Albanians loyal to the state of Serbia. I spoke to most of them, I asked them what it was all about, and they said, You will never understand this. We simply have to do that. Years passed by and I don't remember many names. Also, I don't want to mention many names because I don't want them to get hurt by their own ethnic groups since by this time they have moved on to other jobs. But I will mention a specific case of my very good work-mate, a comrade who attended Serbian parties, marriages, burials as well, this was Fadil Abazi, he was the head of the so-called All People's Defence, it was a formation within the SUP of Pristina. His wife was also employed with the SUP of Pristina in the analytical department. When the people had begun leaving, he tried to leave the SUP as quietly as possible as well, and after that I met him in the street. I asked him, Fajo, since that was his nickname, what was it that prompted you to join that group? I knew him as a loyal citizen and his father was a policeman in Pec as well. He said, Well, you cannot do anything against sheer force. That was his explanation. Therefore, any further discussion was useless. They were trying to be fair, but they were clearly trying to steer clear of that topic. Perhaps I can expand a bit further. Concerning their walk-out, it was also a difficult time for me since I had a number of colleagues that I shared good and bad with. They left and they simply abandoned me, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, if we continue this way we won't be able to cover some important topics. We've been talking about this for ten minutes and we've only come up with a single name.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: I can mention the names of 90 per cent of the people I remember. Practically all of them who had been employed left. I failed to answer an important issue, which is a number of Albanians who remained, they never left. Among those, there was a number of Albanians who were tasked with staying to pass on information from within the state institutions on behalf of the illegal government of Kosovo and Metohija. This was proven at a later stage. Some of my colleagues were later identified as KLA executioners. I believe that is necessary to mention. If you want me to mention names, I will gladly do so. I can explain it graphically, including the events that those so-called colleagues participated in. They used to be diligent detectives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. So you say that the KLA existed in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, I was born in that very area, the central part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a question that demands a yes or no answer. Do you say that the KLA existed in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even before that, but under a different name. If I may, I can tell you when they officially came out for the first time as the KLA because I was immediately involved in the shedding light on the murder at the border crossing in Glogovac when the current prime minister, Thaqi, since he was the right hand of Adem Demaqi and a few other extremists, killed some of my colleagues who were driving to work in a van. The very next year, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was 1993. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will go back to that if there will be any need to do so, but can you tell us what the names of the people who stayed in the police are?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: For example, there were departments, for example, the crime police or the uniformed police, and in those there were certain Siptars, a certain number of Siptars. I cannot speculate as to any exact figures, but I'd say some 10 per cent or more. They were in all departments at all levels. None of them was moved or removed from their positions. Many were even promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just -- no, no, we'll come to it later. Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us of some examples after the Yugoslav forces had withdrawn, what the fate of some of those people who stayed to work for the police was?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: What period of withdrawal do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1999, but briefly please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: In the area of Glogovac, and I will speak only of my policemen although I could expand that to include the SUP of Pristina since I worked there as well, however, in the OUP of Glogovac Xhafer Qorri, assistant commander was killed. After several attempts which had failed by the KLA to kill him and his family, he was final killed -- well, there are documents, as far as I recall. It is the 11th of November and we can go back to the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 11th of November in which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] November -- the 11th of November, 1998, I'm still in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what the question's about. The question you were asked is about the fate of policemen who stayed after the forces withdrew in 1999. If Mr. Lukic wants to ask you about 1998, he'll go back to that. He wants to know about the Albanian police officers who stayed behind after June 1999 and what their fate was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the withdrawal of the Serb forces and the events during 1999, a number of Albanian policemen went into hiding, mainly in Skopje, so as to escape the KLA revenge. A number of them went into retirement. Ahmet Bruna, who was a police colonel, was in hiding for a period of time and he retired, he also spent some time in Serbia, in Belgrade, in some Scandinavian countries as well. I have direct knowledge of that since we were also friends apart from being colleagues. Hamza Hajra was a detective of mine in Glogovac. He was hiding in Skopje for a while and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell us about the ones that were killed or kidnapped or anything of that nature for remaining behind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was about to before you interrupted me, Your Honour. I wanted to tell you of Hamza Hajra. There was an attempt on his life for three times, but finally he was killed in 2001 when he tried to go back to Glogovac since he was born there. He was killed in a vehicle together with his wife and three children. They were massacred in the bloodiest of ways. He was an Albanian who was truly loyal, a good worker, and tried to go back to his place of birth. He was killed with his entire family. He was simply destroyed. Killed would be putting it too lightly. All those who stayed within the service, they had to leave Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us just in brief terms how was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A group of KLA members opened fire from several directions on the vehicle he was driving in with his entire family. Only by pure chance did a single child survive. They were all killed in the centre of Glogovac. There is abundant documentation in existence and I believe international forces also verified that and conducted an on-site investigation. As far as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What others were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Xhafer Qorri was killed, although that was before the end of the war and they tried to kill his entire family as well. Qerim Qshishku, assistant commander, managed to flee Kosovo and Metohija, and I don't know in which country he is now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were any others killed after June 1999 that you can identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Glogovac, where I was, two of those who stayed were killed, the rest fled, trying to save their skins and families. That is put in the briefest possible of terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who were these two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Xhafer Qorri was assistant commander of the police station in Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not talking about 1998. We're talking about after June 1999. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how many more were killed after June 1999 because they stayed behind in Kosovo and were targets for revenge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hamza Hajra was killed in 2001 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had him, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rest did not return and there were so few of them left they were not killed, their numbers were limited in the service in that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. So there is one example of a policeman who remained being killed after May -- June 1999 that you can identify. Can you now help me with a different question. Can you tell me of - and if you need to go into private session we'll do that - Albanian police officers who left Kosovo with the forces which left in June 1999? Can you give me some names? And if you want to protect their privacy we'll go into private session. Now, do you have names of such people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zenel Hoti --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Should we hear this from you in private rather than in open court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it can be in public session since this is a well-known fact. In the meantime he returned to Kosovo and Metohija, although I don't know where exactly. As far as I know, he does reside in Kosovo and Metohija. Zenel Hoti worked in Glogovac for a while. He was a detective. Then in the SUP of Pristina until 1999, when he withdrew with our units, I think he worked for the SUP in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you say he now lives in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, for two years now he's been living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any who have left permanently as of May or June 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many left. A lot of time has passed, and I cannot recall all of the names, but, for example, Tolaj, a traffic policeman, first name Ismet, he retired from the SUP in Belgrade, he was an Albanian. He wasn't the only one. Many of them retired in the end after working in the SUPs of Serbia proper. I remember him, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he -- but they worked in Kosovo right up until June 1999; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they withdrew together with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. So that's one. Are there others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I say, I've forgotten most of the names because there were too many to remember. In each of the SUPs there was someone, one of the members of the Albanian ethnic minority or the Gorani or whoever, Muslims, people who adhered to Islam, the numbers were enormous. Another example that I can now remember was Mujo Kujovic, who also retired from the Belgrade SUP. He happens to be a Muslim. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is he an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're Muslims. Ismet Tolaj is an Albanian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Kosovo Albanians. Now, you've given me one name. Can you give me any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- well, only those I personally socialised with and those who were around me, those are the only people I can remember, and I don't know their names. I used to meet them a lot, but I really don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just have a question for you. Now, you said that people abandoned their jobs. You also said that some retired. Now, when you talk of abandoning of the jobs, does it mean they just went away and were absent from their job or did they resign? And about retirement, you mean they retired in due course, which is reaching a certain age. So what do you mean by this, can you kindly clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Yes, yes. I understand you clearly. Some -- for example, if you look at where I worked directly, a police officer who after the first clashes in Likosane was directly involved and was a very good police officer, really, I can't for the life of me remember his name, there might be some documents to that effect, he never spoke to anyone, never got back to anyone, he just left for Switzerland in order not to be subjected to any pressure by his own people. Because he had family over there, his brothers who were working there. Qerim Qshishku, as I say, assistant commander had been working as inspector for a long time, assistant inspector, very capable. In 1999 when he had already received threats that something would be destroyed he was very open with me that they would crush his family, destroy his family. There was an attempt on his life, and he never got back to anyone -- well, that was the usual. I know that they applied they never spoke to anyone. He just left. For example, something that we call he left and nobody knew where he went to, someone else who abandoned his post Medo Agovic for example, another Muslim from Milica near Pec, one of the police officers from our original team at the time his family was still in Pec, they were in danger, and he said -- I cannot continue to work here anymore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean -- I didn't ask for the reasons why they did all that. I'm just saying what was the modus, whether they resigned, whether they just left without leaving a leave application, and about those who retired whether they retired because of the age or having served for such long. That's the only question I've asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, fine, that's fine, that's fine. The gist is this, those who left, they didn't announce that to anyone. We were extremely tolerant in that sense. We crossed the threshold, the legal threshold, and were ready to take responsibility for that all in the belief that they would soon return when we heard that they had left in order to go abroad and that they were not to return, and then as they say it was the final --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's okay. I have understood. What about those --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Let me just say something else about your question. In the case of retirement, this was perfectly legal once they had reached a legal age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to be retired and there is not a single case that I am aware of. You see what I am saying that someone was retired before they had reached their legal age limit or in any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, I really appreciate your knowledge, the sheer depth and breadth of your knowledge, but let me be very graphic about where we stand right now. I've asked you a hundred questions and you've answered two. We've used up a lot of time. If we go on like this, you'll end up answer maybe a grand total of four of my questions. I will simply have to put an end to this exercise. Therefore, could you please focus, answer my questions, we cannot go on like this, it is entirely impossible, because the Rules of this court do not allow for anything like that. Please focus, answer my questions. Can we press on, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you were born in Glogovac. Which area is that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: The Drenica area, and again I have to as they --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just please, as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: The Drenica area, yeah, sure as briefly as I can. The documents about the Drenica area go back to before the Turks invaded the area of Kosovo and Metohija. Other than that, the well-known Emperor Vuk Brankovic ruled the area, he was born in Trstenik, which is a mere 5 metres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to intervene at this stage. The rules here are quite clear. I don't know what your experience is of courts elsewhere, perhaps in your own home country, but in this court you answer the questions that you are asked. Now, you were asked a very simple question, which area is Glogovac in and you answered it in three words: The Drenica area. Mr. Lukic will now ask you what he wants to ask you next. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Briefly, please, three or four sentences if you can about the more recent history, the problems in this area, they date back to when exactly and who was it who fought who else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: The Drenica area after the Second World War Srez which is the centre of Drenica's administration after World War II was Srbica and Glogovac. Comprising today's Srbica area and Glogovac area. So this is the main stronghold in the Drenica area. Between World War II and the 1990s in both Glogovac and Srbica, as they say, at the top positions in the administrative sense in Srez and in the municipalities there were only Albanians and their deputies were Serbs. Likewise, I can tell you briefly, if you like, about that explains something more about that. You can't view this in isolation. I mean, Glogovac municipality is isolated from Srbica municipality, it's all one thing, that's how the people see it, both Serbs and Albanians alike. Here I'll name you an example, the typical example. After World War II the first president was a man named Bajram Trnavac, who was a president of the Srez, S-r-e-z.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, we simply cannot go on like this, we really cannot. Why was the command staff at the Glogovac OUP replaced? If you keep on being as expansive as you've so far been, we simply will not be able to go on.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC
utterances.text: There had been frequent terror attacks on citizens and state bodies in Glogovac.
